case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the Helms‑Burton Act allows a U.S. national who acquired ownership of a certified claim after the statutory cutoff date to sue cruise lines for “trafficking” in confiscated Cuban property, or instead bars such suits unless the plaintiff acquired the claim before March 12, 1996.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (the Helms‑Burton Act), 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A) (cause of action for U.S. nationals who own claims to confiscated property; liability for persons who “traffic” in such property), including the Act’s related eligibility/limitations language tied to March 12, 1996.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Havana Docks argues that Title III’s cause of action extends to any current U.S. national who owns the claim, regardless of when the claim was acquired, and that the statute’s March 12, 1996 language should not be read to categorically bar assignees/successors who acquired the claim later; on this reading, cruise lines that used the Havana docks in Cuba “trafficked” in confiscated property and are subject to damages, consistent with Congress’s deterrent and remedial purposes and U.S. foreign-policy interests in discouraging commercial exploitation of expropriated American property.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents contend that Title III imposes a temporal/anti-trafficking standing limitation keyed to March 12, 1996—i.e., plaintiffs may sue only if they acquired the claim (or owned the claim) before that date—so post‑1996 acquisitions cannot support Title III liability; they argue this is the best reading of the statutory text and structure, avoids opening U.S. courts to a broad secondary market in Cuban-expropriation claims, mitigates foreign-relations and international-comity concerns, and prevents expansive, retroactive liability for routine travel and commerce connected to Cuba.

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point is that § 6082(a)(1)(A), read in isolation, allows any current U.S. national who “owns the claim” to sue, so present ownership should suffice. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito explain, § 6082(a)(4)(B) speaks directly to who may “bring an action” on pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations and conditions that authority on when the plaintiff “acquired ownership of the claim,” making the date-certain cutoff an express eligibility rule. Reading (a)(1)(A) to swallow (a)(4)(B) would turn the general cause-of-action grant into an all-purpose hook and drain the later, specific limitation of operative effect. On text and structure, the threshold question is plaintiff-class eligibility, and Congress drew a clear line that this plaintiff cannot satisfy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point is that § 6082(a)(1)(A) authorizes suit by any U.S. national who “owns the claim,” which, read in isolation, could be taken to include later assignees. But, as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice explain, § 6082(a)(4)(B) speaks directly to the threshold entitlement to “bring an action” on pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations and makes the acquisition date an express condition of the right Congress created. We are not at liberty to treat that date-certain limitation as surplusage or a mere merits consideration; when Congress defines the eligible plaintiff class for a statutory cause of action, that limitation is part of the right itself. Enforcing the cutoff as written also avoids enlarging the statute’s waiver-like authorization beyond its stated terms by permitting post-1996 assignments to manufacture eligibility.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest argument for Petitioner is that § 6082(a)(1)(A) authorizes suit by any current U.S. national who “owns the claim,” so later-acquired claims should qualify. But as the Chief notes, that reading would override—and largely nullify—the specific eligibility restriction in § 6082(a)(4)(B), which bars suits on pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations unless the plaintiff acquired ownership of the claim before that date. Justice Kagan’s point about integrating the cause-of-action provision with the cutoff best reflects ordinary statutory interpretation: the general grant in (a)(1) is conditioned by the later, more specific limitation in (a)(4). Given the foreign-relations sensitivity and Congress’s evident choice to prevent a post-1996 market in assignments engineered to generate litigation, we should enforce the cutoff as written rather than expand Title III beyond Congress’s delineated bounds.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point is that § 6082(a)(1)(A) speaks in the present tense—any U.S. national who “owns the claim” may sue—suggesting later-acquired ownership could suffice. But, as Justice Kagan and the Chief explain, § 6082(a)(4)(B) is a distinct, express gatekeeping provision that bars a national from “bring[ing] an action” on pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations unless the national acquired ownership before that date; reading (a)(1)(A) to override that limitation would render Congress’s date-certain line largely surplusage. Given the statute’s calibrated structure and its foreign-relations backdrop, I do not read this congressionally crafted exception to authorize a substantial expansion via post-1996 assignments absent clear textual direction. The administrable, constraint-oriented approach is to enforce the cutoff as an eligibility condition defining the plaintiff class, which the respondent has not met.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point is that § 6082(a)(1)(A) authorizes suit by any current U.S. national who “owns the claim,” which, in isolation, could include later assignees and better serve deterrence. But as the Chief Justice explains, § 6082(a)(4) speaks directly to who may “bring an action” and makes that authority turn on when the plaintiff “acquired ownership of the claim,” with March 12, 1996 doing non-optional gatekeeping work for pre-1996 confiscations. Reading (a)(1)(A)’s general ownership language to override (a)(4)’s specific temporal condition would largely nullify Congress’s date-certain limitation—an atextual move our whole-act approach forbids. If Congress wished to permit post-1996 assignees to sue, it could have said so, and we should not expand the plaintiff class by implication.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point remains that § 6082(a)(1)(A) authorizes suit by any U.S. national who presently “owns the claim,” which—if read in isolation—might include later assignees. But, as the Chief Justice explains, Congress immediately cabins who may “bring an action” in § 6082(a)(4)(B) by making timely acquisition (before March 12, 1996) an express prerequisite for suits on pre–1996 confiscations; reading (a)(1)(A) to swallow that specific gate would render the date-certain limitation largely surplusage. I also find Justice Kagan’s integration point persuasive: the general cause-of-action grant is conditioned by the later, more specific eligibility restriction, and nothing in the Act supplies an “as if” transition device extending Title III to after-acquired claims. On these facts, Havana Docks’ post-1996 acquisition places it outside the enumerated plaintiff class Congress opened the courthouse doors to.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point is that § 6082(a)(1)(A) authorizes suit by any current U.S. national who “owns the claim,” suggesting present ownership alone is enough. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, § 6082(a)(4)(B) is the more specific, directly applicable provision governing who may “bring an action” on pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations, and it makes acquisition timing an express eligibility condition. Reading (a)(1)(A) to trump (a)(4)(B) would effectively nullify Congress’s date-certain cutoff and invite the post-enactment assignments Congress plausibly meant to foreclose—an administrable line we should respect, especially in a foreign-relations-sensitive statute. On an institutionalist, restraint-oriented approach, we apply the statute Congress wrote; any expansion to later assignees is for Congress, not us.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point is the present-tense phrasing in § 6082(a)(1)(A)—a U.S. national who “owns the claim” may sue—suggesting current ownership is enough. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 6082(a)(4) speaks in the same operative terms (“may not bring an action … unless”) and supplies a date-certain acquisition prerequisite for pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations; reading (a)(1)(A) to permit post-1996 assignees would drain (a)(4) of force and create a mismatch between the general authorization and Congress’s explicit gatekeeping rule. On an ordinary understanding of a statutory right of action, the plaintiff’s “legal right to file suit” exists only if it satisfies Congress’s defined eligibility conditions, and nothing in the statute indicates Congress meant later assignments to manufacture Title III standing decades after the cutoff. That coherence-based reading avoids the “odd result” of an indefinitely expandable plaintiff class absent any such indication in the text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioner’s best textual point is the present-tense phrasing in § 6082(a)(1)(A) authorizing suit by a U.S. national who “owns the claim,” which, in isolation, could be read to reach later assignees. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, § 6082(a)(4)(B) speaks directly to who may “bring an action” on pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations and makes eligibility turn on whether “such national acquired ownership of the claim” before that date—an express, context-specific temporal gate that would be drained of operative force under petitioner’s reading. Using traditional tools of construction, the specific, date-certain limitation cabins the general cause-of-action language, and absent a clear congressional instruction to authorize post-1996 assignment-based expansion, that policy request is better directed to Congress. Accordingly, respondent has the better reading of the statutory text and structure.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title III’s baseline rule is that private suits are available only on the terms Congress specified, and the March 12, 1996 ownership language operates as a text-bound limitation on who may invoke the cause of action. Reading § 6082(a)(1)(A)’s reference to a current “United States national who owns the claim” to override § 6082(a)(4)’s cutoff would convert a targeted eligibility restriction into an all-purpose hook, effectively authorizing a secondary market in post-1996 assignments that Congress plausibly sought to foreclose. Consistent with separating threshold eligibility from merits, the question here is not whether cruise lines “trafficked,” but whether this plaintiff may sue at all—and the statute’s structure indicates Congress conditioned that jurisdiction-invoking right on pre–March 12, 1996 acquisition. Absent a clear statement that Congress meant to permit later-acquired claims to sue, we should not treat Title III as a radical expansion of private enforcement with significant foreign-relations consequences.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The operative text of Title III ties who may sue to a temporal ownership/acquisition condition keyed to March 12, 1996, and that eligibility limitation does real work in defining the class of plaintiffs Congress authorized to invoke this cause of action. Reading the statute as allowing any current owner—regardless of when the claim was acquired—would effectively nullify Congress’s expressed cutoff and convert a limited, carefully delineated remedy into one that can be freely expanded through post-1996 assignments. Because Congress created the cause of action against traffickers and simultaneously specified who qualifies to sue, that cutoff is best treated as an integral condition of the right to sue that must be applied as written, not relaxed in light of broader deterrent purposes. On these facts, a U.S. national who acquired a certified claim after March 12, 1996 is outside the statutorily authorized class and therefore cannot maintain a Title III action against the cruise lines for alleged trafficking.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Title III creates a cause of action only within the express limits Congress set, and § 6082(a)(4)(B) states that, for pre–March 12, 1996 confiscations, a U.S. national may not bring an action “on a claim to the confiscated property unless such national acquired ownership of the claim” before that date. Reading the statute as Petitioner urges would effectively nullify that cutoff and invite a post-1996 secondary market in assignments—an expansion of the remedy beyond the bounds Congress delineated for who may sue and when. The Act’s structure repeatedly keys liability, authorization, and damages to “claim” ownership, confirming that Congress meant to restrict standing based on acquisition timing rather than simply current possession of a claim. In a statute touching sensitive foreign-relations concerns, we should enforce those explicit limitations rather than extend Title III’s private damages remedy absent a clear congressional directive.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title III’s cause of action is a carefully cabined exception that Congress tied to specific eligibility conditions, including temporal limits keyed to March 12, 1996, and we must enforce those gatekeeping requirements as written rather than treat them as open-ended remedial purposes. Reading the statute to allow post‑1996 assignees to sue whenever they later become U.S. nationals who “own” a certified claim would substantially expand the set of eligible plaintiffs, inviting a secondary market in claims and opening U.S. courts far beyond Congress’s calibrated design. The statutory structure’s use of the cutoff date functions as a strict threshold condition on who may bring suit, and the plaintiff’s post‑1996 acquisition fails that element. Against the backdrop of foreign-relations sensitivity and Congress’s decision to create a limited exception rather than a radical departure, the better reading bars this action.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The place to start is Title III’s text, and it contains an explicit eligibility restriction keyed to March 12, 1996: Congress limited who may “bring an action” based on when the plaintiff “acquired ownership of the claim,” not merely whether the plaintiff owns it today. Reading the cause-of-action provision together with that cutoff as an integrated scheme, the statute contemplates a temporal gate on plaintiffs—so courts may not create an atextual exception for later assignees simply because doing so would further deterrence. And because Congress spoke directly to this threshold limitation, there is no warrant to override it by policy concerns about trafficking or by inferring broader coverage from the Act’s purposes. On these facts, a U.S. national who obtained the certified claim after March 12, 1996 is outside the class Congress made eligible to sue cruise lines for “trafficking” under Title III.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Title III creates a cause of action only for a U.S. national who both “owns the claim to such property” and satisfies Congress’s express timing condition keyed to March 12, 1996; that date-certain limitation functions as an eligibility rule defining the class of plaintiffs the statute is open to, not a mere damages or proof provision. Reading the provision in its full structure—where Congress enumerates who may sue and then adds a specific acquisition cutoff—post-1996 assignees fall outside the statute’s defined plaintiff class, and ineligibility under the cause-of-action subsection is dispositive absent some separate textual hook (none appears here). Nor does the Act supply an “as if” transitional device or other retroactivity instruction extending the new cause of action to later-acquired claims; instead, the explicit cutoff indicates Congress meant to cabin the private right of action to those holding the claim by the specified date. Because Havana Docks acquired the certified claim after March 12, 1996, it cannot invoke § 6082(a)(1)(A) against the cruise lines even assuming their conduct otherwise qualifies as “trafficking.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The best reading of Title III’s text and structure ties eligibility to sue to ownership of the claim as of the March 12, 1996 cutoff, reflecting Congress’s evident decision to limit this new federal cause of action and to prevent a market in post‑enactment claim acquisitions designed to generate litigation. Interpreting the statute to allow post‑1996 assignees to sue would expand liability beyond what Congress authorized, raise serious practical and foreign-relations/comity concerns that Congress plausibly sought to manage through the cutoff, and risk substantial retroactive exposure for conduct long after confiscation. Consistent with judicial restraint and respect for Congress’s line-drawing, courts should enforce the temporal limitation as written rather than broaden Title III by inference from general remedial purposes. That approach is also more workable administratively because it supplies a clear, objective rule for who may sue.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Title III’s cause of action is keyed not just to current ownership of a claim but to Congress’s express temporal limitation tied to March 12, 1996; reading the statute’s eligibility language in its ordinary legal sense, the “right of action” belongs only to a U.S. national whose claim was acquired/owned by that cutoff, not to later purchasers in a secondary market. That construction best fits the statute’s overall scheme by making the right to sue “mature” only for the class Congress specified, rather than letting plaintiffs create new Title III plaintiffs decades later by assignment—an interpretation that would effectively allow indefinite expansion of liability absent any such indication in the text. And it avoids the structural mismatch that would occur if the Act’s carefully chosen cutoff date had no operative limiting role on who may sue while trafficking liability continues to attach to the same underlying confiscation. In close analogy to exhaustion/limitations cases, the statute should be read to make judicial relief legally available only when the statutory prerequisites are satisfied, not whenever a claim is later acquired.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Hewing to Title III’s enacted text and structure, Congress tied eligibility to sue to a specific temporal gate—ownership of the claim as of (or acquisition before) March 12, 1996—rather than adopting an open-ended cause of action for any later assignee who happens to hold the claim today. Using traditional tools of statutory construction, that date functions as a context-specific eligibility/limitations condition within the remedial scheme, and courts should not treat it as surplusage by reading the statute to permit post-cutoff acquisitions to sue anyway. Because expanding the cause of action to after-acquired claims would materially broaden liability beyond what Congress clearly prescribed—and because clear statutory clarity is required for that consequence—the request to open Title III to a secondary market in claims is better directed to Congress. On these facts, a plaintiff who acquired the certified claim after the cutoff is outside the class Congress authorized to bring this trafficking action.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the Helms-Burton Act allows a U.S. national who acquired ownership of an expropriation claim after March 12, 1996 to sue for trafficking in that claim, or whether the Act bars such suits unless the plaintiff owned the claim continuously since before that date.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (the Helms-Burton Act), principally 22 U.S.C. § 6082(a)(1)(A) (civil remedy for trafficking) and the Act’s temporal limitation tied to March 12, 1996 (commonly litigated as § 6082(a)(4), addressing when a U.S. national may bring an action depending on when the claim was acquired).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Havana Docks argues that the statutory text authorizes suit by “any United States national who owns the claim” and that the March 12, 1996 date limitation should not be read to require that the same person (or entity) have owned the claim continuously since before that date. In petitioner’s view, the Eleventh Circuit adopted an atextual, overly restrictive continuity-of-ownership rule that undermines Congress’s remedial and deterrent purposes, blocks legitimate successors-in-interest (including corporate successors/assignees), and improperly narrows Title III’s reach against entities that profit from confiscated Cuban property. Petitioner also relies on the United States’ position that Title III was designed to be an effective private-enforcement mechanism aligned with U.S. foreign-policy objectives.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The cruise-line respondents contend that Title III’s March 12, 1996 limitation was intended to cabin liability and prevent a market in Cuban expropriation claims, and that the best reading of the statute requires a plaintiff to have held the claim since before that cutoff (or otherwise satisfy the statute’s acquisition-timing restriction). They argue the Eleventh Circuit correctly interpreted the Act to bar suits by plaintiffs who acquired the claim after the statutory date, warning that petitioner’s interpretation would greatly expand exposure for travel and tourism companies, invite opportunistic transfers designed to manufacture standing, and create serious foreign-relations and practical consequences that Congress sought to avoid through the temporal limitation.

John Roberts.reasoning: I remain with Respondent because §6082(a)(4) speaks in plaintiff-eligibility terms—“may not bring an action … unless such national acquired ownership … before March 12, 1996”—and that language most naturally keys the cutoff to the would-be plaintiff’s own acquisition, not some predecessor’s. Justice Jackson’s fairness concern about ordinary succession is substantial, but it cannot justify a reading that would let post-1996 purchasers sue on any pre-1996 confiscation and thereby largely nullify the gatekeeping work Congress enacted; Justice Kagan and Justice Alito correctly stress that petitioner’s approach would invite the very claim-trafficking market the bright-line date was designed to prevent. Read in context as a calibrated, foreign-relations-sensitive remedial scheme, Title III’s broad authorization in (a)(1)(A) must be harmonized with (a)(4)’s limiting condition rather than used to drain it of effect. A narrower opinion can acknowledge bona fide succession concerns and reserve whether certain non-opportunistic transfers might qualify as not “acquir[ing]” within (a)(4), but on these facts petitioner’s post-cutoff acquisition places it outside the class Congress authorized to sue.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Jackson is right that §6082(a)(1)(A) speaks broadly of "any United States national who owns the claim" and that successors-in-interest are often treated as standing in the prior owner’s shoes. But §6082(a)(4) "otherwise provide[s]" a specific, date-certain condition on who "may bring an action," keyed to whether "such national acquired ownership" before March 12, 1996; that is an express limitation Congress wrote into the cause of action, and we must give it operative effect. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, petitioner’s reading would largely nullify the cutoff by permitting post-1996 purchasers to sue whenever a pre-1996 owner once held the claim, inviting the very claim-trafficking Congress sought to prevent. Whatever equitable concerns about routine succession, our task is to enforce the statute’s textual limits on the class Congress authorized to sue, and petitioner falls outside that class on these facts.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that §6082(a)(1)(A) speaks broadly of “any United States national who owns the claim,” and that reading §6082(a)(4) to require continuous ownership risks sweeping in ordinary successions like estates or mergers. But §6082(a)(4) is not an implied limitation; it is enacted gatekeeping text—“may not bring an action … unless such national acquired ownership … before March 12, 1996”—and, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress, petitioner’s reading would largely nullify that date-certain boundary by permitting post-1996 purchasers to sue whenever an earlier holder met the cutoff. Given Congress’s evident aim to prevent claim trafficking through a bright-line temporal limit, and absent a clear statement authorizing post-cutoff acquirers to sue notwithstanding that restriction in a foreign-relations-sensitive scheme, we should enforce the eligibility line Congress drew. Any narrow accommodation for bona fide succession is for Congress to specify, not for us to create in a way that erodes the cutoff’s administrable force.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Jackson is right to emphasize that §6082(a)(1)(A) speaks broadly of “any United States national who owns the claim,” and that successors ordinarily stand in the assignor’s shoes. But §6082(a)(4) is an internal limiting element Congress chose to cabin a highly sensitive cause of action: it states a U.S. national “may not bring an action” unless that national “acquired ownership” before March 12, 1996—language most naturally keyed to the would-be plaintiff’s acquisition, not some predecessor’s. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress, petitioner’s reading would make the date-certain bar do little work because post-cutoff purchasers could reliably manufacture eligibility by purchasing old claims, a “radical departure” from the statute’s evident anti-trafficking design without a clear statement. Jackson’s concern about ordinary inheritance or corporate reorganization may be real at the margins, but absent textual accommodation it cannot justify reading (a)(4) into near nullity in a scheme Congress calibrated against foreign-relations consequences.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson is right to stress that §6082(a)(1)(A)’s authorization—“any United States national who owns the claim”—sounds capacious and that claims are often transferable absent a clear statutory bar. But §6082(a)(4) supplies that bar in plaintiff-eligibility terms: a U.S. national “may not bring an action” on a claim “acquired” after March 12, 1996, which most naturally keys to when the would-be plaintiff acquired the claim, not when some prior owner did. As the Chief Justice underscored, petitioner’s reading would make the cutoff largely self-defeating by allowing post-1996 purchasers to buy pre-1996 claims and sue, draining enacted text of independent work. Jackson’s succession/estate hypotheticals may raise hard edges, but absent an express successor carveout (and given Congress’s evident anti-trafficking design), we should enforce the bright-line condition Congress wrote rather than create an atextual exception.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson rightly emphasizes that §6082(a)(1)(A) authorizes suit by “any United States national who owns the claim,” and that successors-in-interest are ordinarily included absent a clear statutory restriction. But §6082(a)(4) supplies that restriction in plaintiff-eligibility terms: a U.S. national “may not bring an action” unless “such national acquired ownership of the claim” before March 12, 1996—language that most naturally points to the would-be plaintiff’s own acquisition date, not some predecessor’s. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress, reading (a)(4) to be satisfied whenever the confiscation predates 1996 would largely empty the cutoff of independent force and invite the very post‑1996 claim trafficking Congress drew a bright line to deter. Any concern about hard cases involving inheritance or reorganization cannot justify rewriting the condition Congress enacted; it is for Congress to carve exceptions if it wishes.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that §6082(a)(1)(A) broadly authorizes suit by any U.S. national who “owns the claim,” and that successors-in-interest ordinarily may enforce the same claim absent a clear prohibition. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, §6082(a)(4) is precisely that prohibition: it is framed as plaintiff-eligibility language (“may not bring an action”) keyed to when “such national acquired ownership,” which most naturally refers to the would-be plaintiff’s acquisition date, not some predecessor’s. Reading (a)(4) to be satisfied whenever any earlier holder owned the claim before 1996 would largely drain Congress’s bright-line cutoff of independent force and invite the claim-trafficking market Congress sought to prevent. Fairness concerns about routine succession are real, but absent clearer textual carveouts, we should enforce the integrated gatekeeping design Congress enacted rather than create an implied successor exception that risks swallowing the rule.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Jackson is right to stress that §6082(a)(1)(A) is broad—“any United States national who owns the claim”—and that successors in interest ordinarily may sue absent a clear limitation. But §6082(a)(4) is written as exactly that limitation: it says a U.S. national “may not bring an action” if it “acquires ownership of the claim” after March 12, 1996, which most naturally keys eligibility to the would-be plaintiff’s acquisition date, not a prior holder’s. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, petitioner’s reading would let parties recreate eligibility through post-1996 assignments, largely nullifying the cutoff and producing an odd, easily evaded gatekeeping regime. Fairness concerns about routine succession cannot justify reading (a)(4)’s acquisition-date bar as satisfied by someone else’s pre-1996 ownership when Congress framed the condition in plaintiff-facing “may not bring” terms.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take seriously the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s core point that §6082(a)(4) must do real work, and I agree we cannot read the March 12, 1996 cutoff out of the statute. But their reading effectively adds a continuous-plaintiff-identity requirement that Congress did not clearly write, sweeping in ordinary successions (inheritance, mergers) and producing arbitrary forfeiture of a remedial right without improving administrability. Section (a)(4) can still function as anti-trafficking gatekeeping by focusing on whether the claim is one Congress meant to be privately enforceable (i.e., a pre-1996 claim held by a U.S. national in the relevant sense), while leaving courts and the political branches to police opportunistic claim-trading through the statute’s other limitations and suspension authority. Because the statutory text does not plainly say that any post-cutoff transfer—no matter how routine—extinguishes the ability to sue, I would not infer that harsh consequence here.

John Roberts.reasoning: The text, read in context and against the Act’s evident anti-claim-trading design, ties the right to sue to when “the United States national” acquired “ownership of the claim,” using March 12, 1996 as a gatekeeping cutoff that would be largely defeated if post‑1996 assignees could sue so long as someone once held the claim earlier. That broader reading would convert a targeted temporal limitation into an all-purpose mechanism for manufacturing Title III liability through later transfers—an outcome difficult to reconcile with Congress’s effort to cabin the remedy and avoid creating a market in confiscation claims. The statute’s structure suggests Congress drew a line between pre‑existing holders (who could sue) and later acquirers (who generally could not), preserving that basic dichotomy rather than allowing it to be circumvented by assignment. On these facts—where the plaintiff’s ownership postdates the cutoff—the better reading is that Title III bars the action absent qualifying pre‑cutoff ownership by the plaintiff itself (or satisfaction of the statute’s limited timing pathways).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The dispositive question is what Title III’s text makes a condition of the cause of action. While §6082(a)(1)(A) imposes liability to “any United States national who owns the claim,” Congress “otherwise provided” in the same section by adding an acquisition-date limitation keyed to March 12, 1996, and that temporal condition must be enforced as written rather than diluted by policy arguments about deterrence. Read in statutory context, the cutoff operates as an express limit on who may invoke the remedial authorization (i.e., it bars suits premised on claims acquired after the cutoff), which is consistent with Congress’s deliberate use of a date-certain restriction to prevent trafficking in claims themselves. Because petitioner acquired the claim after March 12, 1996, it falls outside the class of plaintiffs Congress authorized to sue, and the action must be dismissed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The question is controlled by the limits Congress expressly built into Title III’s cause of action, and § 6082(a)(4)’s March 12, 1996 acquisition cutoff is a clear temporal boundary that cabins who may sue, not an invitation to expand liability through later assignments. Reading § 6082(a)(1)(A)’s “any United States national who owns the claim” to permit post‑1996 acquirers to sue would largely nullify Congress’s chosen date line and create an easily manipulated market in claims, precisely the sort of open-ended expansion beyond the remedy Congress delineated that I have resisted in prior cases. A bright-line rule requiring the plaintiff to have owned the claim before (and continuously since) March 12, 1996 is administrable and respects the statute’s structural design choice to condition the remedy on acquisition timing. Especially given the foreign-relations sensitivity and the statute’s interaction with conduct involving foreign property, I would not broaden Title III’s reach absent a clear statement overriding that temporal limitation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Reading Title III’s text and structure against its legal and historical backdrop, the March 12, 1996 acquisition limitation functions as a meaningful internal constraint on this extraordinary cause of action—one Congress designed with foreign-relations and reciprocity consequences in mind. Petitioner’s reading (“any U.S. national who owns the claim” regardless of when acquired) would largely nullify the temporal limitation by allowing post‑cutoff purchases and assignments to manufacture Title III standing, a major and unintended expansion of liability that Congress did not clearly authorize. The better construction gives the cutoff real work: only a U.S. national who held the claim before March 12, 1996 (and thus not someone who acquired it later) may sue for trafficking, which avoids creating a market in expropriation claims and cabins the statute’s reach as Congress sought to do. On these facts—where the plaintiff acquired the claim after the cutoff—the Act bars the suit.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title III’s cause of action is broad in §6082(a)(1)(A), but Congress elsewhere added an express acquisition-date restriction keyed to March 12, 1996; reading the statute as a whole, that specific temporal limitation qualifies who may “bring an action,” and it would be odd to treat it as doing no work whenever a claim is later assigned. Under a text-first approach and ordinary structural reasoning, a provision that conditions suit on when “the United States national” acquired the claim most naturally requires the plaintiff to have owned it by (and since) the cutoff, rather than allowing post-cutoff purchasers to sue merely because they now “own” a claim. And because this restriction functions as a gatekeeping eligibility rule rather than a remedial measure, I would not dilute it based on Title III’s deterrent purposes absent clearer statutory language authorizing suits by later acquirers—especially given the evident congressional concern about creating a market in such claims. Against the backdrop of federal statutes that sometimes restrict standing to specified holders at specified times, I would enforce the temporal limit Congress wrote, not replace it with a more expansive policy-driven rule.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The enacted text couples Title III’s cause of action for “any United States national who owns the claim” with an express acquisition-date limitation keyed to March 12, 1996, and that temporal line would do little work if a plaintiff could satisfy it by purchasing an old claim at any later time. Reading the provisions as an integrated package, the most natural way to give effect to Congress’s explicit cutoff is to require that the plaintiff’s ownership trace to (and thus be held since) before the statutory date, not merely that the underlying confiscation predated it. Statutory structure and expressio unius also point the same direction: Congress specified who may sue and imposed a specific temporal qualification, and courts are not free to dilute that condition in the name of broader remedial purpose. On these facts, where the plaintiff acquired the claim after March 12, 1996, the Act’s timing restriction bars the action.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Start with the operative text: Title III generally authorizes suit by a U.S. national who “owns the claim,” but Congress added a specific temporal limitation keyed to March 12, 1996 that provides a U.S. national “may not bring an action” on a confiscated-property claim acquired after that date. Reading the Act as a whole, that cutoff functions as a structural channeling/limiting provision—part of Congress’s design to cabin Title III liability and to prevent an administratively unworkable market in claim-trafficking and opportunistic post-enactment transfers designed to manufacture Title III plaintiffs. Petitioner’s reading would largely drain the cutoff of practical effect by permitting parties to acquire old claims long after 1996 and then sue based solely on current ownership, a sweeping consequence that Congress did not clearly authorize in the limiting language it chose. And absent an unmistakable statement, I would not adopt an interpretation that creates that kind of broad expansion of liability with significant foreign-relations and systemic consequences when Congress instead wrote a bright-line acquisition restriction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Start with the text. Although § 6082(a)(1)(A) creates liability for trafficking against “any person” and authorizes suit by a U.S. national who “owns the claim,” § 6082(a)(4)’s March 12, 1996 cutoff functions as a claimant-eligibility limitation that turns on when the plaintiff became legally entitled to sue on that particular claim. Reading (a)(1) to allow any post-1996 purchaser to sue would let parties manufacture a matured “right to file a civil action” by assignment and would largely nullify Congress’s evident effort to prevent a market in these claims—an “odd result” in light of the statute’s integrated scheme tying the remedy to a fixed temporal baseline. Harmonizing the provisions, Title III is best read to require that the plaintiff’s ownership trace to (and, in substance, persist from) the pre–March 12, 1996 date, so a U.S. national who acquired the claim only after that date may not sue for trafficking in it.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title III’s operative liability provision authorizes suit by “any United States national who owns the claim,” and reading § 6082(a)(4)’s March 12, 1996 language as a rigid, implied continuous-ownership rule would add atextual restrictions that undermine Congress’s chosen private-enforcement mechanism. From a procedural-fairness standpoint, the better interpretation is one that treats successors-in-interest and assignees as able to vindicate the same claim, absent a clear statutory command to the contrary, because otherwise similarly situated victims of confiscation are arbitrarily barred based on post-1996 corporate succession or estate transfer. Pragmatically, while respondents’ concerns about opportunistic claim-trading are not trivial, Congress addressed temporal and foreign-relations sensitivities through express limitations and executive-branch suspension authority, and courts should not expand those limits in a way that defeats remedial deterrence against ongoing trafficking. On these facts—where the plaintiff alleges current trafficking in a confiscated-property claim—the statute’s text and practical consequences favor allowing suit by the current owner of the claim even if acquired after March 12, 1996.
